DEFAULT.title: DEFAULT · Warm Contemporary
DEFAULT.tagline: Bed faces the balcony, wardrobe fills the alcove, study-dresser on the thick wall.
DEFAULT.why: It uses every piece of the L-shaped room for what it is best at. The 5'4" x 3'4" alcove beside the door is exactly the size of a 3-door wardrobe, so storage costs no floor space. The bed sits on the only long solid wall (east) and faces the 10'5" balcony opening, giving the best view and morning light. The 7'3" thick south wall becomes a study-cum-dresser. That leaves a clear 5'8" zone between the bed and the balcony and a 3'10" walkway from the door. Aluminium sliders, laminate and vitrified tile are standard, affordable and low-maintenance in Indian conditions.

OPTION_D.title: Option D · Smart Budget (Indian)
OPTION_D.tagline: The same well-planned layout as DEFAULT for about ₹1,93,300: ready-made pieces, a local carpenter and colour instead of costly finishes.
OPTION_D.why: Money goes where it lasts and gets used every day: a full-height wardrobe with a loft, proper aluminium sliders for the balcony and the window, and a good mattress. It saves on things that cost a lot but add little: no false ceiling, no panelling, no veneer or acrylic, and the existing floor stays. The look comes from colour and Indian textiles: a terracotta accent wall, indigo cotton curtains, a handloom dhurrie, a cane moodha and a Madhubani print. Walnut and frosty-white laminate tie the carpenter work to the ready-made bed. The layout is DEFAULT's, which already works: bed facing the balcony, wardrobe in the alcove, study-dresser on the thick wall.

OPTION_E.title: Option E · Simple & Practical
OPTION_E.tagline: About ₹1,47,900 as recommended (₹1,28,400 with the 'Within ₹1.3 lakh' pick): plain paint, a sliding wardrobe with the mirror on its door, a standing desk. ✏️ Customise changes the 3D, colours and budget.
OPTION_E.why: This is how an interior designer keeps a small bedroom on a budget: spend on what you use every day (a good wardrobe, bed, mattress, a proper desk, a fan and good light) and skip what only looks fancy. The walls are simply painted: one washable paint, two shades. Nothing hangs from the ceiling except the fan and lights, the builder's windows stay, and no furniture stands in a walkway. Unlike DEFAULT there is no lounge chair: this room has no free spot where a chair can be used without blocking the path beside the bed. You sit at the desk, on the bed, or later on the balcony.

sections.Layout: Bed centred on the east wall (the only long solid wall), facing the balcony. One bedside on the window side and a floating shelf on the door side, so both walkways stay about 2'2" wide. Standing desk and a pegboard on the thick wall. Sliding wardrobe with the full-length mirror on its door, right by the room's entrance. Fan over the foot of the bed. 5' of open floor between the bed and the balcony door.
sections.Wardrobe & mirror: Sliding doors, because the wardrobe sits right at the room's entrance: hinged doors would swing into your path. The mirror goes on the front sliding door, so you dress where your clothes are and it throws balcony light into the alcove. The wall that had the mirror becomes a pegboard for your bag, headphones and keys. Prefer to see the whole wardrobe at once? Choose hinged doors in ✏️ Customise.
sections.Ceiling (bare concrete now): Your ceiling is the underside of the RCC roof slab. It needs: ~12 mm gypsum plaster (punning) to make it smooth → putty → primer → 2 coats ceiling-white paint. Before plastering, fix the fan hook (anchor fastener rated for a fan) and run the light wires in thin surface conduits, because RCC can't be cut for pipes. If the flat has a terrace above, get the roof waterproofed and coated with heat-reflective white paint first.
sections.Walls & paint: One washable emulsion everywhere (Asian Paints Apcolite Premium or a Berger / Nerolac equivalent, matt or low-sheen). Warm off-white on three walls, pale sage on the bed wall, ceiling white. Process: fill cracks → sand → primer on the patches → 2 coats. If the walls are still grey cement, they need 2 full coats of putty first (choose 'Bare cement plaster' in ✏️ Customise).
sections.Lighting & fan: 1200 mm BLDC fan (~30 W, with remote). 4 surface LED panels (4000K) placed away from the pillows, 2 warm wall reading lights, a 20 W LED batten under the desk shelf. AC point and pipe sleeve done now for a split AC later.
sections.Standing desk: Single-motor electric sit-stand desk, 4'×2', with memory presets. Set the standing height so your elbows are at 90° (about 3'5" for someone 5'6"–5'8"); sitting height about 2'4". Monitor top at eye level. Anti-fatigue mat; the mesh chair tucks under when you stand.
sections.Window & door: The builder's aluminium sliders are kept (clean the tracks, oil the rollers). A pleated mosquito mesh is added to the balcony door. Beige blackout eyelet curtains on plain SS rods. Upgrade W1 to a uPVC tilt-and-turn window in ✏️ Customise if you want quieter, dust-tight, rain-safe ventilation.
sections.Palette: Warm off-white, pale sage, light oak, white, beige, denim blue. Change any of them in ✏️ Customise.

ROOM2_ENSUITE.title: V1.2 · Room 2 En-suite (bath with tub)
ROOM2_ENSUITE.tagline: A wall across the north end of Room 2 turns Bath 2 and a new tub room into one bathroom, with a single door into Room 2.
ROOM2_ENSUITE.why: Bath 2 already opens only into Room 2, and Room 2 is the longest room (23'7"). A 5" wall 4'11" from the north wall makes a tub room right next to Bath 2. The old Bath 2 doorway stays open, so the WC and the tub room work as one bathroom. The only way in or out is the new 2'6" door. The wall can't go further south: the east window W5 starts 5'5" from the north wall.

PU/cementitious coat on the tub-room floor, 1' up all walls and 3' up around the tub
Anti-skid matt vitrified 600×600, ~62 sq ft, ½" lower than Room 2 with a floor trap
Matt 300×600 to 7' (~220 sq ft) + sage feature tile behind the tub

budget.savings: If it runs over: a basic 1500 mm acrylic tub (about ₹18,000), a plain diverter instead of a thermostatic mixer, ceramic wall tiles and a ready-made PVC vanity bring it to about ₹1.5 lakh.

sections.Layout: Tub room 12'7" (north) narrowing to 12'2" × 4'11" clear. Tub in the NE corner along the north wall. Vanity with a mirror on the new wall, beside the door. Geyser high on the west wall. Bath 2 (4'5" × 7'1") keeps the WC and a small hand basin, reached through its old doorway, which now has no door leaf.
sections.One door: The new door is in the new wall, 9" from Room 2's west wall. It opens into the bathroom and its hinge is on the east jamb, so the open door lies along the wall and doesn't block the Bath 2 doorway or the vanity. Room 2 has no other bathroom door.
sections.Bathtub: 1500 × 750 mm acrylic soaking tub (about 180 L) dropped into a tiled masonry surround on a 4" plinth. The plinth gives the waste pipe its fall to the Bath 2 stack. Wall mixer with a diverter, a spout and a hand shower on a slide rail, so the tub doubles as a shower. A PEVA curtain on a rod keeps splashes in.
sections.Water & waterproofing: The tub room floor is ½" lower than Room 2 and falls to a floor trap beside the tub, with a granite threshold at the door. Waterproof the whole floor, 1' up every wall and 3' up around the tub before tiling. Hot and cold supply in CPVC, waste in PVC to the existing Bath 2 stack through the shared west wall.
sections.Light & air: Window W4 is now the bathroom window, so it gets frosted film. The existing high vent above the tub takes a 150 mm exhaust fan. Two IP44 downlights plus a mirror light, all 3000K warm white. A 15 L geyser on its own 16 A point.
sections.Room 2 after the change: Room 2 becomes 18'3" long, 12'1" wide at the new wall narrowing to 10'6". It keeps both east windows (W5 and W6) and both doors to the passage and the hall. It loses the north window W4 to the bathroom.
sections.Palette: Warm grey matt tiles to 7', a sage-green feature wall behind the tub, oak vanity, white sanitaryware, chrome fittings.

HALL_REC.title: V1.3 · Recommended
HALL_REC.tagline: Matt GVT tiles through the flat, an 8 ft WPC fluted TV wall with a metal frame, anti-skid bathrooms and Kota outside.
HALL_REC.why: My pick for most families: it looks finished, needs almost no upkeep and sits in the middle on cost. The main door (3 ft, middle of the hall's west wall) opens into an entry with a shoe cabinet. The TV wall sits north of the door, centred under the beam; the dining table sits south, near window W7.

rows: Matt GVT 600×1200 in hall, passage, Room 2 and kitchen; anti-skid R11 in the bathrooms; Kota in the open square (installed)
Premium washable emulsion over putty and primer, about 900 sq ft
WPC fluted panel 8 ft × 8'5" (about 70 sq ft), black aluminium frame, LED strip
304 steel corner guards on both pillars
budget.note: Furniture, lights and the fan are drawn for the layout and are not in this total. Rough 2026 estimates, not quotes.

sections.Pros:
• Matt tile hides Bihar's dust and is safe with wet feet
  • One tile through the flat makes it look bigger
  • WPC is waterproof and termite-proof and hides the TV wires
  • Almost no upkeep: mop and wipe
sections.Cons:
• A deep chip in GVT shows the body colour (keep a spare box)
  • WPC looks like wood from far, not up close
  • Paint needs redoing every 6–8 years
sections.How long it lasts:
• Floor tiles: 15–25 years
  • WPC TV wall: 12–15 years
  • Premium paint: 6–8 years before a repaint
sections.Verdict: Best value. Pick this unless money is very tight or you want to build once for 25 years.

HALL_BUDGET.title: V1.3 · Budget plain
HALL_BUDGET.tagline: Double-charge tiles, plain washable paint, a TV on the wall and nothing extra. Room 1 shows Option D (Smart Budget).
HALL_BUDGET.why: Spends money only where it lasts: tough tiles, anti-skid bathrooms and Kota outside. Everything else can be upgraded later without breaking anything. The main door (3 ft, middle of the hall's west wall) opens into an entry with a shoe cabinet. The TV wall sits north of the door, centred under the beam; the dining table sits south, near window W7.

rows: Double-charge vitrified 600×600 in hall, passage, Room 2 and kitchen; anti-skid R11 in the bathrooms; Kota in the open square (installed)
Economy washable emulsion (for example Asian Paints Tractor Emulsion or Berger Bison Glow), about 900 sq ft
Wall bracket, PVC wire casing, laminated shelf
budget.note: Furniture, lights and the fan are drawn for the layout and are not in this total. Rough 2026 estimates, not quotes.

sections.Pros:
• Lowest cost
  • Double-charge tile is very tough and small chips barely show
  • Nothing to maintain except paint
  • Add the WPC TV wall later without touching the floor
sections.Cons:
• Plain look; 2 × 2 ft tiles show more joints
  • Few stone or wood looks in double charge
  • Economy paint needs redoing every 4–5 years
  • Visible TV wires unless cased
sections.How long it lasts:
• Floor tiles: 20–25 years
  • Economy paint: 4–5 years before a repaint
sections.Verdict: Pick this if money is tight now. The floor will outlast the Recommended one; the looks can come later.

HALL_LONG.title: V1.3 · Long-lasting
HALL_LONG.tagline: Full-body vitrified floors, a porcelain-slab TV wall with steel profiles and steel guards. Built once, left alone for 25 years.
HALL_LONG.why: For a family that wants to do the work once. Every surface is the toughest of its kind: colour that runs through the tile, a wall finish that never fades or swells, and stainless steel that never rusts. The main door (3 ft, middle of the hall's west wall) opens into an entry with a shoe cabinet. The TV wall sits north of the door, centred under the beam; the dining table sits south, near window W7.

rows: Full-body vitrified 600×1200 matt in hall, passage, Room 2 and kitchen; anti-skid R11 in the bathrooms; Kota in the open square (installed)
4 inch full-body tile skirting, whole flat
Premium washable emulsion over putty and primer, about 900 sq ft
Porcelain slabs 800×1600 (about 70 sq ft) with 304 brushed steel profiles, granite-top console
304 steel corner guards to 5 ft on both pillars
budget.note: Furniture, lights and the fan are drawn for the layout and are not in this total. Rough 2026 estimates, not quotes.

sections.Pros:
• Longest life of any tile: chips and scratches hardly show
  • Porcelain slab wall is waterproof, fade-proof and wipes clean
  • Stainless steel profiles and guards never rust
  • Nothing to polish, seal or replace
sections.Cons:
• About ₹35,000–60,000 more than Recommended
  • Large slabs need a skilled mason and careful handling
  • Hard to change the look later
  • Fewer designs in full-body tiles
sections.How long it lasts:
• Floor tiles: 25–30+ years
  • Porcelain TV wall: 25+ years
  • Steel trims: life of the flat
  • Paint: 6–8 years
sections.Verdict: Pick this if you want to build once and not touch the hall for 20–25 years. It costs more up front but has the lowest cost over time.

HALL_MARBLE.title: V1.3 · Marble classic
HALL_MARBLE.tagline: Indian white marble in the hall and passage with a green border, a limewash TV wall with teak shelves. Room 1 shows Option C (Indian Modern).
HALL_MARBLE.why: The traditional look many Bihar homes love: seamless polished marble, cool in summer, that can be re-polished to look new. The rest of the flat stays on matt GVT to keep cost and upkeep down. The main door (3 ft, middle of the hall's west wall) opens into an entry with a shoe cabinet. The TV wall sits north of the door, centred under the beam; the dining table sits south, near window W7.

rows: Indian white marble (Rajnagar / Makrana) in hall and passage, ground and polished; matt GVT in Room 2 and kitchen; anti-skid in the bathrooms; Kota in the open square (installed)
6 inch green marble border inlay round the hall
4 inch marble / tile skirting, whole flat
Premium washable emulsion over putty and primer, about 900 sq ft
Limewash feature wall 8 ft wide in warm clay, four solid teak floating shelves
304 steel corner guards on both pillars
budget.note: Furniture, lights and the fan are drawn for the layout and are not in this total. Rough 2026 estimates, not quotes.

sections.Pros:
• Classic, seamless look with no grout grid
  • Can be ground and re-polished to look new again
  • Cool underfoot in Bihar's summer
  • Limewash and teak feel warm and natural
sections.Cons:
• Stains from haldi and oil, etches from lemon and curd
  • Icy in winter; needs rugs
  • Re-polish every 8–12 years; hard water dulls it
  • Most expensive here and slowest to lay
sections.How long it lasts:
• Marble: 50+ years, with a re-polish every 8–12 years
  • Limewash: recoat every 5–8 years
  • Teak shelves: decades with occasional polish
sections.Verdict: Pick this only if the family really wants marble and is ready for the upkeep. For the same look with far less work, use glossy marble-look tiles in the hall instead.

HALL_PANEL.title: V1.3 · Panelled hall
HALL_PANEL.tagline: The whole TV wall in fluted WPC, 3 ft sage half-wall panelling with a champagne aluminium cap round the hall, and both pillars wrapped full height.
HALL_PANEL.why: For a warm, finished, hotel-lobby look. The panels protect the lower walls from mops, chairs and scuffs, so only the top half ever needs paint. Floors are the same matt GVT as the Recommended plan. The main door (3 ft, middle of the west wall) opens between the TV wall and the entry shoe cabinet.

rows: Matt GVT 600×1200 in hall, passage, Room 2 and kitchen; anti-skid R11 in the bathrooms; Kota in the open square (installed)
4 inch tile skirting outside the hall
Premium washable emulsion above the panels
Fluted WPC on the whole wall north of the door (about 110 sq ft), black profile, LED strip
3 ft WPC / HDHMR panels with moulding strips, about 160 sq ft, champagne aluminium cap
Both pillars wrapped full height in fluted WPC (about 72 sq ft)
budget.note: Furniture, lights and the fan are drawn for the layout and are not in this total. Rough 2026 estimates, not quotes. Panel prices vary a lot between makes: get the panel brand and thickness written on the quote.

sections.Pros:
• Warm, premium look with no extra furniture
  • Half-wall panels take the knocks from mops, chairs and shoes; the lower wall never needs repainting
  • WPC is waterproof and termite-proof, and hides uneven plaster and wiring
  • Wrapped pillars stop chipped corners and look intentional
sections.Cons:
• The most panel work, so one of the costliest plans
  • Panels hide the wall: fix any damp first, or it will spread behind them
  • Dust settles in the flutes; dust them weekly
  • A lot of wood tone can feel heavy; keep the rest of the walls light
sections.How long it lasts:
• WPC feature wall and pillar wraps: 12–15 years
  • Half-wall panels: 10–15 years
  • Floor tiles: 15–25 years
  • Paint above the panels: 6–8 years
sections.Verdict: Pick this if you love panelling and the walls are dry. For a lighter budget, keep only the fluted TV wall (the Recommended plan) and add half-wall panels later.

HALL_BEST.title: V1.4 · Best of both
HALL_BEST.tagline: Smooth matt GVT (2×4 ft in the hall and passage, 2×2 ft in the rooms), one flat laminate TV panel over a low cabinet, a tile band at the entry, steel pillar guards and a slim gypsum border with cove light.
HALL_BEST.why: This mixes my guide's Bihar-proof floor and wall picks with the Materials Field Guide's cheaper, easier-to-clean TV wall, its caution on tile size and its ceiling advice. Every surface is smooth, so there are no grooves to dust. The tub room geyser is now 50 L, because a 15 L geyser cannot fill the tub.

rows: Smooth matt GVT: 600×1200 in the hall and passage, 600×600 in Room 2 and the kitchen, same shade; anti-skid R11 in the bathrooms; Kota in the open square (installed)
Washable emulsion over putty and primer, about 900 sq ft
Flat matt HPL laminate (light oak) on 18 mm BWP plywood, 7 × 7 ft, black top profile, LED strip
3'6" matt wall tile on the entry wall (about 47 sq ft), aluminium top trim
2 ft gypsum border on GI framing round the hall (about 170 sq ft) with cove LED
budget.note: Skip the gypsum border and the total drops to about ₹1,93,000–3,20,000. Furniture, lights, the fan, mesh doors and the geyser are not in this total. Rough 2026 estimates at Patna rates, not quotes; outside Patna add transport.

sections.Pros:
• Smooth faces everywhere: no grooves collecting dust
  • 2×2 tiles in the rooms are easy for a local mason; 2×4 only where it shows
  • TV wall costs about half of a WPC fluted wall and is easy to change later
  • Entry wall takes shoe and bag knocks; pillar corners don't chip
  • The border hides wiring and gives soft evening light
sections.Cons:
• Laminate looks flatter than real wood or fluting
  • The border lowers the ceiling edge and adds joints to look after
  • Two tile sizes mean two orders in the same shade: match the batch codes
  • Costs a little more than Recommended because of the ceiling
sections.How long it lasts:
• Floor tiles: 15–25 years
  • Laminate TV panel: about 10–15 years if the wall stays dry (estimate)
  • Gypsum border: 15–20 years without leaks, repainted with the walls
  • Paint: 6–8 years
  • Steel guards and tile band: for life
sections.Also plan:
• Mosquito mesh doors: hinged, aluminium frame, replaceable mesh. Fit one room first
  • Tub room geyser: 50 L (shown in the model)
  • Before buying tiles, take two samples home and test tea, haldi and oil on them
sections.Verdict: My pick now: the best mix of looks, easy cleaning and cost. If money is tight, drop the ceiling border first.
